title: Relative marked reversal, mapping objects and cartesian horns
statement:
Use simplicial sets, functor objects and universes of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], marked simplicial sets, $K^\flat,K^\sharp$, marked products and model-category conventions of [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], and the opposite $K^{\mathrm{op}}$ of [lem-coef-simplicial-opposite-homotopy-calculus]. Extend the inner-fibration and cartesian/cocartesian edge horn definitions of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations] to arbitrary simplicial bases: cartesian edges solve final-horn problems for every $n\geq2$ with prescribed edge $\{n-1,n\}$, and a cartesian fibration has cartesian lifts with prescribed target of every base edge; cocartesian means the initial-horn and prescribed-source conditions. No quasicategory hypothesis on total space or base is imposed. The natural marking $Z^\natural$ of a cartesian (respectively cocartesian) fibration $Z\to S$ marks exactly its cartesian (respectively cocartesian) edges, its distinguished edges; $\operatorname{Fun}_{/S}(X,Y)_n$ is the set of simplicial maps $X\times\Delta^n\to Y$ over $S$, with operators acting on $\Delta^n$, whether or not the total spaces are quasicategories. For a small base $S$ let $\mathsf M_S$ be the category of marked simplicial sets over $S$, and define $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_S(X,Y)_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf M_S}(X\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp,Y)$. Put $O_S(X,M)=(X^{\mathrm{op}},M)$ over $S^{\mathrm{op}}$, retaining the same degree-one subset of marked edges. Then $O_S:\mathsf M_S\to\mathsf M_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}$ is an equivalence with inverse $O_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}$, preserving degreewise limits, colimits and monomorphisms. It exchanges cartesian and cocartesian fibrations, their natural markings and maps preserving their distinguished edges. There are natural isomorphisms
$$\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}(O_SX,O_SY)\cong(\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_S(X,Y))^{\mathrm{op}},\qquad O_S(X\times K^\sharp)\cong O_SX\times(K^{\mathrm{op}})^\sharp.$$
These respect identities, composition, tensors and their right adjoint cotensors, and restrict to opposite isomorphisms on the full simplicial subsets of $\operatorname{Fun}_{/S}(X,Y)$ spanned by distinguished-edge-preserving maps and on their cores. If $i\mathbin{\square}j$ denotes the pushout product of a marked map $i$ and an unmarked map $j:K\to L$, using tensor $X\times K^\sharp$, then $O_S(i\mathbin{\square}j)\cong O_S(i)\mathbin{\square}j^{\mathrm{op}}$. For every $a:T\to S$, composition $a_!$ and degreewise pullback $a^*$ satisfy $O_Sa_!\cong(a^{\mathrm{op}})_!O_T$ and $O_Ta^*\cong(a^{\mathrm{op}})^*O_S$, compatibly with their adjunction units and counits. The same reversal identifies vertex fibers with their opposites.

proof.text: Use the degreewise involution of [lem-coef-simplicial-opposite-homotopy-calculus]. Since the unique operator from $[1]$ to $[0]$ is fixed by reversal, the degenerate edges of $X$ and $X^{\mathrm{op}}$ are the same subset of $X_1$. Thus retaining $M$ gives a marked object, and a marked map remains marked because its degree-one component is unchanged. The equations expressing a map over $S$ become those over $S^{\mathrm{op}}$. Applying reversal twice restores every operator, marking and base map, so $O_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}O_S=1$ and $O_SO_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}=1$ on objects and arrows.

In a small limit diagram over $S$, take the underlying limit in each degree; mark an edge precisely when every projection is marked. A compatible cone of marked maps factors through this object as a marked map, uniquely. For a colimit use the underlying degreewise colimit over $S$ and mark the images of all marked edges; these contain all degenerate edges, and the cocone universal property is again immediate. These descriptions include the empty limit $S^\sharp$ and empty colimit $\varnothing$. Reversal leaves these sets, projections, cocone maps and marking tests unchanged, so preserves their universal maps. It also preserves products with marked objects by the coordinatewise marking rule. A marked map is monic exactly when each underlying component is injective: injections cancel degreewise; conversely two different $n$-simplices with equal images give two different maps from $(\Delta^n)^\flat$ over $S$ that it equalizes. This characterizes monomorphisms and proves their preservation and reflection.

For an inner fibration $p:E\to S$, reversal preserves inner fibrations and identifies a final horn $\Lambda_n^n$ with the initial horn $\Lambda_0^n$, by [lem-coef-simplicial-opposite-homotopy-calculus]. Its vertex identification sends the specified ordered edge $\{n-1,n\}$ to $\{0,1\}$. Applying the involution to the entire lifting square gives a bijection of these horn problems and of their fillers. Thus an edge is $p$-cartesian exactly when its opposite is $p^{\mathrm{op}}$-cocartesian, using the outer-horn definitions of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations] extended in the statement. A base edge with prescribed target reverses to one with prescribed source at the same degree-zero element. Hence the lift-existence clauses also correspond. Marking exactly these edges and testing a map on each such edge now proves the natural-marking and distinguished-edge-preservation clauses. The argument never fills a horn in $E$ or $S$ separately, so neither is assumed to be a quasicategory.

proof.text:
Let $\theta_n:\Delta^n\to(\Delta^n)^{\mathrm{op}}$ send an $m$-simplex $\beta:[m]\to[n]$ to $\beta^\vee(i)=n-\beta(m-i)$. For $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$, substitution gives $(\Delta\alpha)^{\mathrm{op}}\theta_m=\theta_n\Delta(\alpha^\vee)$. Send a marked relative map $f:X\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\to Y$ to
$$R_n(f)=f^{\mathrm{op}}(1\times\theta_n):O_SX\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\to O_SY.$$
The product marking is preserved since $\theta_n$ has all edges marked. The map is over $S^{\mathrm{op}}$ because the base projection ignores its parameter. Reversal twice is inverse on these sets. The displayed identity implies $(\alpha^\vee)^*R_n(f)=R_m(\alpha^*f)$, or equivalently $\alpha^*R_n(f)=R_m((\alpha^\vee)^*f)$. These are exactly the operators of an isomorphism $(\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_S(X,Y))^{\mathrm{op}}\cong\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}(O_SX,O_SY)$. Restriction in $X$, postcomposition in $Y$, and every base-preserving map commute with the formula.

source.place: §1.2.1; §3.1.3, relative sharp mapping objects before Remark 3.1.3.1

proof.text: Composition in the sharp enrichment sends $f:X\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\to Y$ and $g:Y\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\to Z$ to $g(f(x,t),t)$; the identity is $\operatorname{pr}_X$. This formula is a marked map by the coordinatewise product rule. Reversal commutes with substitution, and $\theta_n$ commutes with the parameter diagonal: both diagonal coordinates are $\theta_n(t)$. Consequently $R_n(g\circ f)=R_n(g)\circ R_n(f)$ and $R_n(1)=1$. For every $K$ the identical pair of degreewise components gives $O_S(X\times K^\sharp)=O_SX\times(K^{\mathrm{op}})^\sharp$, including markings. The unit parameter, product associator, and tensor action maps are the identical coordinate maps, so this equality respects the tensor action and its compatibility with enrichment.

source.place: §3.1.3, mapping-object definitions; agent substitution and product calculation

proof.text:
For $Y\to S$, the right adjoint to $X\mapsto X\times K^\sharp$ exists explicitly as
$$Y^{K}_{/S}=Y^{K^\sharp}\times_{(S^\sharp)^{K^\sharp}}S^\sharp,$$
where the exponentials are the marked internal Homs of [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], and the last map transposes $S^\sharp\times K^\sharp\to S^\sharp$. Transposition says a marked map $Z\to Y^K_{/S}$ over $S$ is precisely a marked map $Z\times K^\sharp\to Y$ whose base map is the projection. For any $W$ over $S^{\mathrm{op}}$, Step 1 and the tensor equality of Step 5 give natural bijections
$$\operatorname{Hom}(W,O_S(Y^K_{/S}))\cong\operatorname{Hom}(O_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}W,Y^K_{/S})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(W\times(K^{\mathrm{op}})^\sharp,O_SY).$$
Transposing the identity maps in these bijections constructs inverse maps between $O_S(Y^K_{/S})$ and $(O_SY)^{K^{\mathrm{op}}}_{/S^{\mathrm{op}}}$. Their composites transpose to identities, proving the cotensor isomorphism. Because the bijections were the explicit marking-preserving transpositions, they intertwine the tensor-cotensor adjunctions, evaluation and coevaluation; the mapping adjunction follows by the same transposition with a simplex parameter.

source.place: §3.1.3, mapping adjunctions and relative exponential formula in Proposition 3.1.3.3; agent transposition calculation

proof.text: Apply the same $R_n$ formula without markings to maps $X\times\Delta^n\to Y$. It restricts the unmarked functor reversal to relative functors, since the equation with the map to $S$ is carried to the equation over $S^{\mathrm{op}}$. In degree zero it sends $u$ to $u^{\mathrm{op}}$. Step 3 shows that $u$ preserves the distinguished edges if and only if $u^{\mathrm{op}}$ preserves their reversed kind. A full simplicial subset consists of the simplices all of whose vertices belong to its chosen object set, by [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]; reversal merely reverses the order of this vertex list. Hence the relative functor reversal restricts to the asserted full subsets. Finally an inverse edge and its two inverse-triangle witnesses reverse to an inverse edge and the two reversed triangles, exchanging the two inverse equations. Therefore the subsets of simplices all of whose edges are equivalences, which define the cores, also correspond. This only compares these simplicial subsets; no Kan assertion for an arbitrary relative functor object is used.

source.place: §1.2.1; §3.1.3 and Remark 3.1.3.1; agent restriction to full subsets and inverse-triangle witnesses

proof.text:
Write $i:A\to B$ over $S$ and $j:K\to L$. Its pushout product for the sharp tensor is
$$(B\times K^\sharp)\amalg_{A\times K^\sharp}(A\times L^\sharp)\longrightarrow B\times L^\sharp.$$
Apply Step 2 to the displayed pushout and Step 5 to each product. Each resulting corner is the corresponding corner built from $O_SA,O_SB,(K^{\mathrm{op}})^\sharp,(L^{\mathrm{op}})^\sharp$, and each boundary arrow is $O_Si$ or $j^{\mathrm{op}}$ with the unchanged other coordinate. The induced arrow is therefore precisely $O_Si\mathbin{\square}j^{\mathrm{op}}$. This proves the claimed natural pushout-product isomorphism for arbitrary $i,j$, without monomorphism or fibrancy assumptions.

source.place: §3.1.2, pushout-product construction; agent application of Steps 2 and 5

proof.text: For $a:T\to S$, $a_!$ retains the marked object and composes its base map with $a$. Thus $O_Sa_!$ and $(a^{\mathrm{op}})_!O_T$ have identical simplices, markings and base maps. For $Y\to S$, pullback is $T\times_SY$ with a pair marked exactly when its $Y$-edge is marked: view it as the marked pullback $T^\sharp\times_{S^\sharp}Y$. Reversal retains its degreewise equation $a(t)=p(y)$ and that marking test, proving $O_Ta^*=(a^{\mathrm{op}})^*O_S$. A map $a_!X\to Y$ corresponds under adjunction to $x\mapsto(p_X(x),f(x))$ into the pullback. The unit is $x\mapsto(p_X(x),x)$ and the counit is $(t,y)\mapsto y$. Each formula is unchanged in every degree after reversal, which proves compatibility of both identifications with the adjunction, not just with the functors. For a vertex $s$ the fiber has simplices $y$ with $p(y)$ the constant simplex at $s$; constant simplices reverse to themselves, giving $(X_s)^{\mathrm{op}}=(O_SX)_s$.
